summary: This document specifies the DOTS signal channel, a protocol for a client to signal the need for protection against Distributed Denial-of-Service attacks to a server that can mitigate the traffic. A companion document defines the DOTS data channel. It obsoletes RFC 8782.

eli5.summary: When a website is flooded with fake traffic, it needs a quick way to call for help. This document defines that emergency call.

questions: how does a dots client request ddos mitigation
what is the difference between rfc 9132 and rfc 8782
subtitle: How a network under DDoS attack asks a mitigation provider for help, using small CoAP messages over (D)TLS.

tldr.problem: During a Distributed Denial-of-Service attack, a network owner often cannot tell what is hitting it but still needs to ask a provider that can filter traffic, and the request must get through even when links are congested.
tldr.mechanism: A DOTS client sends CoAP requests over DTLS/UDP or TLS/TCP (default port 4646) to a DOTS server, carrying CBOR-encoded mitigation scopes, with heartbeats and status notifications keeping the channel alive and informative.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9132 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8782, keeping the same CBOR keys while adding a comprehension-optional key range, an error summary and a table of default values.

today: RFC 9132 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8782. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Players
sections.content:
A Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack tries to make machines or network resources unavailable by exhausting something finite: memory, CPU, link capacity or firewall state. Often administrators cannot determine the cause. They only notice that certain resources seem to be under attack.

This RFC defines the DOTS signal channel, a lightweight protocol that lets a DOTS client request mitigation from one or more DOTS servers for detected, suspected or anticipated attacks. In typical deployments the client and server sit in different administrative domains, for example a customer network and a service provider. The server may or may not be co-located with the mitigator that actually filters traffic, and a DOTS gateway can sit in between.

The document follows the DOTS architecture of RFC 8811 and the requirements of RFC 8612. It is the companion of the DOTS data channel, specified in RFC 8783, which handles configuration and bulk data exchange.
sections.eli5: Imagine a shop that gets swamped by thousands of pretend customers. The shop owner phones a security company to say what needs protecting. DOTS is that phone call, made by machines.

sections.title: Design: CoAP over DTLS or TLS
sections.content:
The signal channel is built on the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP). The RFC picks CoAP because it expects packet loss, supports asynchronous Non-confirmable messaging, has congestion control, adds little message overhead and supports (D)TLS. Messages are serialized in CBOR, a compact binary encoding, with the content type application/dots+cbor.

Unless the two sides agree otherwise, the channel MUST run over port 4646 for both UDP and TCP. The RFC chose it instead of the usual secure CoAP port 5684 to avoid the service and resource discovery that CoAP defines and to allow different behavior where a DOTS gateway and an IoT gateway share a box.

By default the DOTS client acts as a CoAP client and the server as a CoAP server, but roles can flip for operations such as heartbeats. DOTS agents MUST support GET, PUT and DELETE. Each operation is a path under /.well-known/dots, and a client can only see the resources it created itself.

Because a middlebox might block UDP or an IPv6 path might be broken, the client uses a Happy Eyeballs style procedure. The preference order is UDP over IPv6, UDP over IPv4, TCP over IPv6, then TCP over IPv4. During an attack the client SHOULD use a Connection Attempt Delay of 100 ms, and it caches the outcome so it does not thrash the network.
sections.eli5: The message goes in a small, sealed envelope and is sent on a special numbered door, 4646. If one road to the provider is blocked, the sender quickly tries the others.

sections.title: Requesting Mitigation
sections.content:
To ask for help, the client sends a CoAP PUT to /.well-known/dots/mitigate. Two Uri-Path parameters identify the request. The cuid is a globally unique Client Unique Identifier that the client generates. The RFC recommends deriving it from a SHA-256 hash of the client's public key information, truncated to 16 bytes and base64url encoded, so that it is 22 characters long. The mid is an integer identifying the mitigation request, and its values MUST increase monotonically.

The body holds a single scope describing what to protect. At least one of target-prefix, target-fqdn, target-uri or alias-name MUST be present. It can also list target-port-range and target-protocol. The mandatory lifetime is in seconds, with 3600 recommended and -1 meaning indefinite, which the server may refuse. A lifetime of 0 is invalid. Setting trigger-mitigation to false creates a preconfigured request that only starts when the signal channel session is lost; it defaults to true.

The server checks that target prefixes belong to the client's domain, and it MUST reject requests with several entries in scope. A new request with a higher mid and an overlapping scope overrides the older one. If a request conflicts with others, the server answers 4.09 (Conflict) or 2.01 (Created) with conflict-information naming the cause and, for deactivated requests, a retry-timer. Behind a server-domain gateway, the gateway adds a cdid (client domain identifier) so the server can apply per-domain policy.
sections.eli5: The request is a form: what to protect, which doors, and for how long. Each form has a number, and a newer form with a bigger number replaces an older one about the same thing.

sections.title: Status, Efficacy Updates and Withdrawal
sections.content:
A client reads back its mitigations with GET. With the CoAP Observe option set to 0, the server pushes notifications whenever the mitigation status changes and periodically in between, because packets are likely to be lost in an attack. These notifications MUST always be Non-confirmable. Without Observe, the client can poll, but never faster than one UDP datagram per round-trip time.

The status value tells the client where things stand, from 1 (setup in progress) to 8 (mitigation will start only if the signal channel is lost). Optional counters report dropped bytes and packets. The client SHOULD react to the server's reported status rather than its own detection, so it does not withdraw a mitigation too early.

While mitigation runs, the client MAY send an efficacy update: a PUT that repeats the original request and adds attack-status (1 for still under attack, 2 for successfully mitigated). It carries an empty If-Match option so that a late-arriving update cannot recreate a mitigation that a DELETE has already removed.

A DELETE with cuid and mid withdraws a mitigation and is answered with 2.02 (Deleted). To avoid flapping, the server MAY keep mitigating for an active-but-terminating period, 120 seconds by default and doubling up to 300 seconds if the client asks again. If mitigation started because the channel was lost, recovery of the channel MUST NOT stop it.
sections.eli5: After calling for help, the client can keep asking, or ask to be told, how it is going. When the attack is over it says thanks, and the helper waits a bit before packing up in case the attackers come back.

sections.title: Session Configuration
sections.content:
Using PUT to /.well-known/dots/config with a sid identifier, a client can negotiate how the channel itself behaves: the heartbeat interval, how many missing heartbeats are tolerated, the probing rate, and CoAP retransmission settings. A GET returns the minimum, maximum and current acceptable values and MUST NOT be relayed by a gateway.

Separate settings can apply while a mitigation is active (mitigating-config) and while idle (idle-config), and agents switch between them automatically. Recommended values are an ack-timeout of 2 seconds, max-retransmit of 3, ack-random-factor of 1.5, a heartbeat-interval of 30 seconds and missing-hb-allowed of 15. Configuration requests use Confirmable messages, unlike mitigation traffic.

The server SHOULD return a Max-Age option to say how long a configuration stays valid. Without one, the client refreshes every 60 seconds. During an active attack clients MUST NOT send refresh requests.
sections.eli5: Before trouble starts, both sides agree on the rules of the phone line: how often to say 'still there?' and how long to wait for an answer.

sections.title: Heartbeats and Redirection
sections.content:
To tell an idle channel from a dead one, each side sends heartbeats: Non-confirmable PUT requests to /.well-known/dots/hb with a peer-hb-status flag saying whether the sender has heard its peer within the last two heartbeat intervals. Heartbeats also keep NAT and firewall state alive. If a DOTS agent gets no response for missing-hb-allowed consecutive heartbeats under normal conditions, it concludes the session is disconnected, and the client tries to reestablish it, preferably by resuming the (D)TLS session, no more often than every 60 seconds.

Link saturation changes the rules. If a massive attack fills the client's incoming link, server replies will be lost even though the client's heartbeats arrive. The client then MUST NOT consider the session terminated, keeps sending over it, and in parallel tries a new session. The server MUST NOT consider the session disconnected while it still receives traffic from the client. If it hears nothing for the full span, it concludes the session is gone and can trigger preconfigured mitigations.

A server can also redirect a client by answering 5.03 (Service Unavailable) with an alternate server name and, optionally, its addresses, plus a Max-Age giving how long to use it. Including addresses lets the client skip a DNS lookup that may itself be under attack. A client redirected to a server it talked to within the last five minutes MUST ignore the redirect, which guards against loops.
sections.eli5: The two sides keep tapping each other on the shoulder. If the taps stop for too long, one of them knows the line went dead. If the line is just jammed, the sender keeps tapping anyway.

sections.title: Security: (D)TLS Profile and Authorization
sections.content:
DOTS agents MUST implement only (D)TLS 1.2 or later and follow the recommendations of RFC 7525. Authenticated encryption MUST be used. Implementations MUST support DTLS record replay detection, stateless session resumption, and either raw public keys or a pre-shared key handshake with (EC)DHE. They SHOULD support TLS False Start and the Cached Information extension to cut delay. A DOTS client verifies the server's certification path and domain name, and includes the server name in the SNI extension.

With (D)TLS 1.3, a client that shared a PSK during idle time can use 0-RTT early data to send a mitigation request in its first message. Servers MUST use the Message ID and Token to detect replay of early data, and the monotonically increasing mid and sid values make replayed older requests fail. DTLS records must also fit in one datagram, so agents assume a path MTU of 1280 bytes if none is discovered, and split long target lists across several requests.

Clients and gateways authenticate each other, and a gateway checks authorization with an AAA server, answering 4.01 (Unauthorized) if the client may not ask for mitigation. A server MUST verify that a client is entitled to act on a given prefix and only act on that client's own domain. If a cuid is guessable, another client in the domain could delete or alter its mitigations, and rate limiting is advised against clients that vary the cuid to exhaust server resources.
sections.eli5: Only trusted callers get through, and each can only ask for help with their own house. Secret handshakes stop copycats from replaying an old call.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 8782
sections.content:
RFC 9132 keeps the CBOR key mapping of RFC 8782, so an attribute has the same key value and CBOR major type in both. The one upgrade required of legacy implementations is to treat the CBOR key range 128-255 as comprehension-optional instead of comprehension-required. That range is anticipated for DOTS telemetry.

Other changes include restructuring the YANG module to follow RFC 8791 (dropping cuid, cdid and sid from the body, since they travel as Uri-Path options), a new section summarizing the error responses a server can return, a new IANA range for comprehension-optional attributes, an appendix of recommended and default values, and subsections in the mitigation text for readability.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. Old players can keep playing; they only need to learn to skip over some new optional cards.

data.title: PUT to request mitigation

items.label: In progress
items.desc: Attack mitigation setup is in progress.

items.label: Attack stopped
items.desc: Attack has stopped and the client can withdraw the request.

items.label: Exceeded capability
items.desc: Attack has exceeded the mitigation provider capability.

items.label: Terminating
items.desc: Client withdrew the request; mitigation is active but terminating.

items.label: Withdrawn by server
items.desc: Attack mitigation is withdrawn by the DOTS server.

items.label: Signal loss only
items.desc: Mitigation starts only if the signal channel session is lost.
